utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, could you -- would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd first inform everyone that Judge Fluegge still, for urgent personal reasons, is still unable to sit, and as we said yesterday, the other Judges find it in the interests of justice to continue to hear this case, under Rule 15 bis. Further, I inform everyone that if there's a little problem with the sound, if certain microphones are switched on, everyone is working hard on it, but it has not been resolved yet. If there are no preliminaries, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Thank you very much. We're ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to now take us briefly to -- to Potocari where, I think we all understand you were working on the 12th and 13th, on those days that the refugees were being transported. And I will soon show you a bit of video that I know you'll recall from the 13th where you're in it. But before we get to that section, can you just tell us, on the 12th and 13th, what was your job in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th and 13th, I was basically leading the Dutch soldiers that were outside the base. The rest of the soldiers and, of course, the officers as well were back inside the base at Potocari, and when I came back from the blocking positions, I basically positioned myself with my soldiers between the -- the refugees. And after the enclave fell and the Serb soldiers came in to our positions, I started leading the Dutch soldiers, helping the refugees and aiding them wherever it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again briefly, did you witness the separations of able-bodied and older men and younger men from their families by the Serb forces in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. During the separations where we, of course, were in the midst of, we saw that Serb soldiers separated able-bodied men from the rest of the refugees, from their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what efforts, if any, did you and your men to do to relieve any of the problems or pressure imposed by that separation?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My soldiers tried to -- to help in every way they could, trying to keep people on their feet, to prevent being trampled on, because of the heat, because of the crowded and chaotic situations. And I myself spoke with Serb commanders and tried to convince them of letting men or young boys and in that state men who were, in my opinion, too old or were not able to be soldiers, Muslim soldiers, to let them go and to leave with their families, to stay with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have any success in influencing the separation -- the lack of separation of some of those younger and older men?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that every time I -- I tried to convince them, it worked, so those men could stay with their families, or those boys were not separated and could stay with their families. But, of course, there were some incidents in grey areas that I still carry with me today, where I did not stand up to them and ask the Serb commanders to let the men go. But basically back to the question, every time I -- I -- I asked them to and try to convince them to let the men stay, it worked, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let's now go to P11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could I ask one additional question. How many times, approximately, did you make such an effort where you succeeded? Was it five times, 20 times, 100 times? Could you give us an indication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's very difficult to estimate, Your Honour, but I think it -- somewhere between 50 and a hundred times a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's now go to the 13th of July, and P1147. And we have the trial video from 05:41 to about 07:00. And I'll stop it occasionally and may ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know this young man in the blue -- blue beret?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a long time ago, but I recognise myself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- let's watch it further then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We've stopped at 06:07:5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This person that we see a bit of the side of his face, that's putting his arm out towards you in a -- he's got a uniform, camouflage jacket on, who was that person known to you as?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the Serb commander I know as Mane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just briefly describe what your communication was with him that day. Just generally.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally during the two days, because this is on the second day, the 13th, but also on the 12th, he made it clear that he was the commander on site, and basically he would tell me when and how many buses or trucks would come, so how many refugees could go and try to board the trucks and the -- and the buses. And I made the arrangement with him on the 12th that basically -- and you cannot really see that in this video because the -- the bulk of the refugees is already -- has already left. But, in the beginning, we had a big group of refugees. We, as UN soldiers, were basically in the middle of them, and helping them, and then just 20 metres away from that were the Serb soldiers, and I made the arrangement with Mane not to mix, so the Serb soldiers would not go to the refugees because we, as UN soldiers, would stand there in the middle of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he identify his commander to you as someone in the -- that showed up in the crowd at some point?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that his commander was known -- I only know the nickname Stalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the identifications and the photographs we'll leave to the 92 ter statement, Mr. President. All right. Let's finish -- let's finish up the short video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Reporter: "Can I ask you something for independent television for Belgrade?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. That's the only section. We'll stop at 06:45:7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'd now like to go to a similar but related topic. Did you have personal contact with General Mladic during these two days while you were in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us in the best deal that you can recall, what, if anything, he said to you or others around you? And just take your time and just describe that as best you can.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first conversation I had with General Mladic was practically a general one about all sorts of topics: The weather, sports, the situation, if I was the commanding officer from DutchBat at the site. And then it gradually changed over to if I was from -- from which country I was, and I was surprised by that question because I thought it was clear that I was from the Netherlands and that DutchBat was from the Netherlands. But, later on, it was clear to me why General Mladic asked me that question because, 2 metres away from the position I was standing and talking to General Mladic, there were a few Dutch soldiers resting, drinking some water, just beside the road. And then he started asking me, and pointing out to those soldiers individually and asking me if they were also from the Netherlands. And he called it Holandija and he said, Is that one also from Holandija? And they were all Caucasian, very Dutch-like looking soldiers, but the last soldier was with a very dark skin. I don't know his heritage but he was one of our soldiers. And he was coloured. And General Mladic asked, when he came up to that soldier and pointed him out to me, and he said -- he didn't ask me where he was from and he said, Well, and that guy, is he from Ethiopia? And I explained to him that that was also a Dutch soldier and that we have a very multi-racial society in the Netherlands and that that worked for us and that that soldier was also a Dutch soldier. General Mladic then told me that that was a -- that he thought that was a big problem for the Netherlands, to have a multi-racial society. And he said to me that in ten years from then - so that was 1995 - in ten years from then, he would be in the Netherlands with his soldiers to help the Dutch and protect them from the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, you remain seated. This is the last warning. If you need to consult with counsel -- Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic. Mr. Mladic remains seated and will be removed from the courtroom because he -- when it happens again, if he stands. What Mr. Mladic does is he expresses with his face agreement or disagreement with what the witness says, and then, if he disagrees, he stands up and asks for consultation. Now you know we have been relatively flexible on the consultations on which we said they could take place only during the breaks. We still allow consultations under two conditions. Mr. Mladic, wait a second. Wait a second until I'm finished. Two conditions. First, Mr. Mladic remains seated; second, he speaks at such volume that no one else in this courtroom can possibly hear him, that is, whispering. If not, consultations are limited to the break again. This happens now again and again. I warned Mr. Mladic several times that he should not stand, which, under circumstances, may have an intimidating effect, which the Chamber does not accept. If Mr. Mladic now wants to consult, under the two conditions - that is, whispering and remain seated - you have an opportunity to have that consultation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can hear Mr. Mladic. He should lower his voice. Otherwise, he will have to wait until the break. Mr. Van Duijn, let's resume where we were. You were telling us about your conversation with Mr. Mladic, especially that he would be in a the Netherlands in ten years from then and to help the Dutch and protect them from ... Could you please resume there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me that he would be in the Netherlands with his soldiers to protect the Dutch from other races and -- and also from Muslims. And I told him that I would -- that I disagreed with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, how was it you were able to communicate in this kind of detail with the general at that point?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point during that conversation, his interpreter, so the Serb interpreter, acted as a liaison between General Mladic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe the other contact and communication you had personally with General Mladic that day.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Late in that day, there was an incident in which I was told and also heard a woman was acting hysterically and also using, at that point, my Muslim interpreter, which was basically the interpreter from the Bravo Company, but, at that time, Captain Groen was already back to the base at Potocari. The interpreter had stayed and helped me during the day. So with the help of that interpreter, I heard that the woman was acting hysterically because she had lost her five children in the crowd. And she thought her five children were still in the crowd, in her back. But, at that point, we stopped the -- the -- the flow of refugees towards the buses and the trucks, and she saw that her five children were already aboard a truck, one of the last trucks of the convoy that was already starting to leave. So we had stopped the flow of refugees and she was still in the middle of them and then was starting to scream and trying to get through the crowd. So we helped her out of the crowd and through the interpreter I heard her story. And, at that point, we still had the arrangement with Mane that we were standing between the refugees and the buses. There was, I think, maybe 50 metres of -- of piece of the road where no one would stand, and then next to the buses, the Serb soldiers would -- would stand, and that was also the point where the singling out of men would happen. So but there were some sort of arrangement that also the Dutch soldiers would not cross over to -- to that -- to that area. For me, it was clear that I wanted to reunite the woman with her five children, and I asked the interpreter if he could help me. I saw General Mladic standing next to the other Serb soldiers basically in that area where I wanted to -- to put the woman into one of the trucks that, as I said, were already leaving. And I knew that he was the only one that could prevent me being shot because I would be crossing a more or less border. So I -- I asked the interpreter to go over to General Mladic and to explain what I was doing, that I was not doing anything drastic or trying to -- to stir up the arrangement but that I was just getting that woman back to her children. The Muslim interpreter hesitated because he didn't want to go over to General Mladic. Of course, I understood him, that he was terrified to do that. But I asked him to help, and I said, Well, I'm going anyway, so if you want to help me, please do that. But I was not sure that he would actually do that. So I picked up the lady and started running and put her into the truck with her five children. And when I turned around, I saw that the interpreter had actually went up to General Mladic and was speaking to him. And based on the fact that I didn't get shot, I concluded that he actually succeeded in convincing General Mladic or keeping the situation as calm as possible. Of course, I went up to my interpreter and to General Mladic to see how that conversation was -- was going, and through the use of my interpreter, General Mladic started telling me that he thought I was crazy for caring and for trying to help Muslim refugees in that way, that he was very angry of the fact, even more angry of the fact, that I had sent a Muslim interpreter to speak to him directly because, at that time, it wasn't clear for him that that the interpreter was speaking on my behalf. And he told me, through the use of my own interpreter, so through the use of the Muslim interpreter, that he would shoot the interpreter on the spot, if that would happen again. Actually, there was also some sort of a sick role play General Mladic started to perform by pulling the interpreter close to his body, put an arm around him and draw him to -- to his body, and he asked me if I knew my own interpreter, and I, of course, was surprised and I said, Yes, of course, it's my own interpreter. And he said, No, you're wrong. The guy that's standing next to me, that's a good guy, that's a stand-up guy, that's a Serb and you should respect him. And he asked me then if I knew him, if I knew General Mladic. And I said, Of course, I know that you are General Mladic. And then he said, No, I'm not General Mladic, I'm a Muslim. I only think of making babies. And I can't remember what he actually said, that he was a bastard or some other swearing words. So this was also what happened during that conversation. All the time my Muslim interpreter had to -- to interpret the things General Mladic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Lastly, I'll go on to one short topic. You have said before that there was a period where you saw documents and materials on the ground. Can you tell us when that was and what you thought that material was?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically after the -- after the footage we have just seen, you could see that the -- the large part of the refugees were already -- had already left, so I had time to focus on other things, which was an incident concerning a water truck and where the Serbs tried to take a water truck away from a place we had some people that were injured and wounded placed, and the Medecins Sans Frontieres were helping them. At that spot, I heard from several people that there -- the situation at that location that we call the White House, just opposite of the entrance of the base at Potocari, was troubling because there were too many men that were singled out, held, and -- and I -- they asked me to take a look there and to -- to see what the situation was. So I went over there, and the commander, Serb commander, Mane and his interpreter also followed me there, and that's where in the lawn of that house, I saw a lot of passports and identity documents and other personal belongings, just in the lawn of that -- of that White House.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you make any comments about that material to anyone?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After assessing the situation and actually seeing that the house was crammed up with singled-out men, I spoke with Mane that was also there on site and ask him -- him why the -- the men could not keep their passports, because the story he had told me earlier about singling out the men had been about they having to check if the Muslim men they had singled out were war criminals, and he told me that the Serbs had a list of possible war criminals and they wanted to know if one of the men was on that list. So I asked him if it -- if the men did not have any identity documents, how they would make sure the identity the men would give was also the true identity. And then he grinned at me and he told me that they -- the men that there were in that house didn't need those documents again. So then it became clear to me that the dark fate that we already thought they would await them became even darker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for coming, once again, to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Ivetic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Van Duijn, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, before I begin with my questions for you I would like to first advise you to play close attention to the actual questions to try to ensure that your answers are directed as closely as possible to my question. And if you don't understand one of my questions, please do not hesitate to bring it to my attention. If that's understood, then we can begin.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right, then. First of all, sir, I'd like to ask you, prior to your deployment to the enclave of Srebrenica in 1995, did you have occasion to receive any instruction or training relative to the specific constitutional or legal framework of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My training prior to the mission was more a military training, and, of course, it took into account the political situation, but that was not the focus of the training which I received. And, of course, I was then a platoon commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You mentioned that the training was more of a military nature. Did it involve any instruction as to the military structure of the Territorial Defence system or the Army of Republika Srpska or the Army of BiH as to their structure and operative rules?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, we had some general information about the basic structure, but the training was more focussed on the area in which we were deployed and the military units we possibly would encounter in the area where we were. So the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And one -- one other item of background before we move to more specifics. I understand that in 1999, that is, after your deployment to the former Yugoslavia was completed, you were promoted to a captain position and served as an intelligence officer in the Royal Dutch Army. And this is from page 5 of your Rule 92 ter transcript, which is Exhibit P1154. What I want to know is if you performed any duties as an intelligence officer while you were deployed in Srebrenica as part of the Dutch battalion?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I do want to focus a little bit more on the training and briefing that you did receive prior to arriving in Srebrenica. First of all, am I correct that as a platoon commander you had 34 men subordinated under you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the number is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while you were 24 years old at the time, most of the men under you would have been an average of 19 to 20 years old; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a good estimation, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that neither you nor the persons under you in your platoon had, prior to Srebrenica, experienced any sort of combat mission or been in a combat zone?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, before you arrived at Srebrenica, am I correct that you and the other soldiers of your platoon and, indeed, of the DutchBat battalion attended a training course for both the air mobile unit that you were in and a special training course for a mission both conducted by the Royal Dutch Army?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to be clear apart from this training that was undertaken on the part of the Royal Dutch Army, you did not undergo any additional or special training from any other UN personnel that were not part of the Royal Dutch Army?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as part of this mission-specific training that you received from the Royal Dutch Army prior to your deployment, am I correct that you also had a introduction to the historical backdrop of the creation of the enclave of Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it also correct that this mission-specific training included instruction on the UN Security Council's special resolution and the cease-fire agreement that applied to the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, after you completed your training and when you deployed to Srebrenica in 1995, did you, as a member of the Dutch battalion, understand your mission to be, in part, aimed at upholding the letter of the Security Council resolution and the cease-fire agreement in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we understood the mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, perhaps could we specify when you are asking about a Security Council resolution and when you're telling us about Security Council resolution, which one do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The 1993 resolution when the enclave was created, Your Honours. I don't have the number off the top of my head but we're about to go into the details of exactly what was specified therein and that the -- I believe the gentleman will confirm those are items that he was instructed to be part of his mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 1993. In which the ... in which the enclave was created. Let's proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Number P23, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P23, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dated 8th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to try now to add some specifics to this general discussion and I think the easiest way to do so would be to direct your attention to some prior testimony that you gave and to see if it is all correct from the Popovic case, 29 September 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can call up in e-court 65 ter number 1D898 and if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you were quite helpful in referring me to me to P23 which is not the Security Council resolution. So, therefore, in order to avoid all kind of misunderstandings, I want to be very precise on what legal instruments are at the basis of your questions and of the answers. P23 is an agreement between Mr. Mladic and Mr. Halilovic about demilitarisation - we have dealt with that briefly yesterday - in which the UNPROFOR was a witness to that agreement and received certain tasks under that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the bases of my questions are entirely upon interviews, statements, prior testimony of this witness that have been disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you're referring to United Nations Security Council resolution, then to hide yourself behind what others have said seems not to be what assists the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could assist Mr. Ivetic and the Chamber, it's -- Resolution 824 is P22, and Resolution 836, P24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they're both 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the reason why I asked which one of 1993. I don't know whether I asked it, but ... Mr. Ivetic, we have two Security Council resolutions in 1993. We have one agreement on demilitarisation. Would you please be very precise in your questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can call up in e-court 65 ter number 1D898. And if we can turn to page 3 of the same, which should correlate to transcript page 2390 of the underlying transcript, and focus then on lines 18 through 22 of the document. There is only one language so if you could perhaps zoom to make it easier for the witness to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if you'll follow along with me, the section I'd like to ask you about begins at line 18 and states as follows: "Q. And I don't want to go through them but under brief headings, that there should be a cease-fire, that the area should be demarcated, that the area should be demilitarised, that paramilitary and military units should leave the area. That was your mission as you understood it, was it? "A. Yes." And, sir, now I have to ask you whether you stand by this selection of your testimony from the Popovic case as being truthful and accurate as to your understanding of the mission you had at the time you were deployed to Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you tell me now, sir, specifically in relation to your understanding that the enclave of Srebrenica should be demilitarised, from where did this understanding come from?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really understand the question, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question, sir. Your understanding that part of the mission involved enforcing that the area should be demilitarised, where did this understanding come from? Was it expressed to you by your superiors? Was it something you read?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A specific part of our training was to uphold and to keep in place the cease-fire and the integrity of the demilitarised zone. So prior to the mission, I was told in -- during our training that this was the -- the situation in the area. And to make a small correction. We did not have the -- nor the power, nor the -- the task to enforce the demilitarisation of the area, just to uphold the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, upon your deployment to the enclave, did you, in fact, have occasion to conclude that the cease-fire was a thing that existed only on paper and was not, in effect, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in the enclave was -- was different from the training we had received prior, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you agree with my statement that there was no actual cease-fire that existed on the ground?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now we will go into more detail later in this aspect but I just want to ask you first: Was it also your appraisal that the enclave had not, in fact, been demilitarised and still had an armed Bosnian Muslim group operating from within it when you deployed?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was still an armed group, an armed Bosnian Muslim group, operating, that's correct. The demilitarisation had not been completed. They started and had -- had some effect, but it was not completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to explore with you a little bit more the issue of demilitarisation of the enclave. And first I'd like to ask you about something that another witness has testified about to see if it is in accord with what you -- your knowledge of what you saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to do so, I'd like to call up Exhibit P00057 in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we have a good practice that we first ask the witness what he knows and, after that, put to him what other witnesses said, if there's any need -- still any need to do so. And I invite you to follow that good practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, was it your experience while on the ground in Srebrenica that as the days progressed, more and more armed Muslim fighters would be seen than previously walking around?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall if we saw, when -- when it comes to numbers, more armed Muslim fighters, but as the days progressed and during the missions -- during the -- the time of the mission, there was more activity on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, when you use the term "activity," I presume you mean military or combat activity. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's accurate. I refer to shootings, detonations, patrols. Military activity, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We -- we started with the presence. That was -- the question was about presence, whether you'd see more armed Muslim fighters. You said, Well, whether there were more or not, activity was more. And you said on both sides. But should I understand, then, that both sides being present, or do you mean combat activity, the Serb forces from outside and the Muslim forces from inside the enclave? Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Serb forces were more active outside the enclave, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And where was their activity directed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes they would shoot at us or just at -- at the town. And the activities we could also see was patrolling or vehicle movements outside the area, and we could see that from our observations -- observation posts. And, of course, we also had some information from inside the enclave and where we were -- where we would be patrolling, we could also get into contact also sometimes by shooting with Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you have occasion to hear about or have knowledge about an incident when some Dutch battalion colleagues were taken captive by the Bosnian Muslim forces at an area known as the Bandera triangle? And, if so, can you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know what the -- the -- the stories were from second-hand. So I heard about those incidents, but that was not in the area I was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The question I do have arising from that is: The Bandera triangle, am I correct that this is a geographic feature that was within the confines of the enclave of Srebrenica which, as you understood it, was supposed to be demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, about the Bandera triangle, we -- I think we've heard some evidence on that, and we established one of these days that there's no dispute about that. Therefore, when Mr. Lukic was invited to put any questions to one of the previous witnesses which would shed new light or would explore new elements he was invited to do so, but that we should not hear, again, the same evidence on a matter which is not in dispute. Looking at the clock, I see it's time for a break anyhow. You might want to consider that for your questions after the break. Mr. Van Duijn, we take a break of 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that the Armija BiH personnel that you saw in the course of your deployment to the Srebrenica enclave, in fact, often had infantry weapons that appeared to be brand new? By infantry weapons, I mean Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say often, but at some stage later on during our mission, we could see that some new weapons were carried by Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to turn to your Rule 92 ter testimony for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P1154. And if we could look for the ninth page of that in e-court, that should correlate to transcript page 2262 in the original numbering. And if we could focus ... I apologise. That does not appear to be the correct page. I'm -- it should be 2262 at the top. So if we could go -- I said the ninth page. I see we're at the 23rd. Should be 2262, the prior page. Thank you. If we could focus now at lines ten through 18 of the -- of the 92 ter transcript that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here, sir, if you could follow along, I do not need to, I think, read it into the record since it's already part of the record. You're talking about the fact that the state of the Dutch infantry weapons that you and other members of the Dutch battalion had access to and describe that due to the weather conditions and that they had been in Srebrenica since the first DutchBat deployment, that they were too old to be used safely, with bullets falling apart and the humidity indicators on rocket-launchers in the danger zone. The question I have for you, sir: Was this the result of an inability to resupply?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the Armija BiH fighters that you saw in the enclave, did they appear to have the same difficulties in relation to their infantry weapons and rocket-launchers as the Dutch side was experiencing or did they seem to have an ability to resupply?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information of the difficulties the Muslim forces had in their resupplying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one follow-up question. Exactly what was the cause of the impossibility to resupply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the actual permits were not given by the Serb forces that were in charge of the -- the OP Papa area, which was the only asphalted road on which the through convoys would enter, if that was possible. But all the convoys basically from March on were not given permission by the -- by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any personal knowledge of that? Is it what you heard? Is it hearsay? What's -- because you testified about it, did you personally experience that to be the reason? Or did you hear it? Could you tell us more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my conversations with the logistics officers, I heard of their difficulties trying to get the clearances and what was needed to -- to -- to address with the Serb forces to -- to get those clearances. And, of course, later on, the disappointment with -- on their behalf when the clearances were not being given. And then we heard also from those logistics officers that the convoys were on their way but stopped at some check-point in another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you have occasion to hear about or witness any UN personnel - and when I say that, I'm not limiting it to DutchBat - supplying or trading with the Bosnian Muslims in relation to weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you about something that you testified about in another case, the Blagojevic and Jokic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we have 65 ter number 1D896. And it should be page 30 in the e-court, which should correlate to transcript page 1102 of that underlying transcript. And if we could focus on line 18 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I will read and invite to you follow along, to follow this section, which bleeds onto the next page and begins as follows: "Q. Okay. But the whole purpose was that this area, this enclave, was going to be protected by the UN and the Serbs were supposed to abide that neutrality in the zone, provided of course that that -- the people inside were totally demilitarised, right? "A. That was the agreement, yes. "Q. That was the agreement. But when you got there on the ground and throughout the whole period that you were there, it was never demilitarised, was it?"

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "A. Not totally, no. "Q. Well, it's like saying a little pregnant, either demilitarised or isn't, right? "A. When you want to demilitarise, then you have -- you need a certain amount of soldiers. You look at the area and being that big when you have so little soldiers, then it's not possible to demilitarise it when you only have 200, 300 fighting soldiers. "Q. All right. But when you're talking about the 200 or 300 fighting soldiers, you're talking about DutchBat; right? "A. Yes. "Q. All right. Of course, this is 1995, it was declared demilitarised back in 1993 so I take it - and it's no fault of DutchBats but everybody that preceded you failed to keep the place demilitarised, right? "A. We knew that the Muslims had arms, yes. "Q. Okay. But my question was everybody that preceded you failed to take away the weapons, right? "A. They didn't take the weapons no." Sir, with respect to this excerpt from your testimony from the other proceeding that I've just read out for you and that you followed along, can you confirm for the record whether this is truthful and accurate as to everything that you said and that you would so say again if asked again under the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's truthful and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can ask one follow-up or two. With respect to the position that the DutchBat did not have sufficient personnel with just 200 or 300 soldiers to demilitarise the enclave, was this something that either you, your colleagues, our your commanders reported upwards to UNPROFOR commanders, whether in Sarajevo or in Zagreb, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that we, in July 1995, only had 2- to 300 soldiers, was also due to the fact that with the humanitarian aid convoys or food or resupplying convoys for DutchBat, also the convoys which took soldiers on their leave were also not able to come back due to the fact of the permission that was not given by the -- the Serb check-points. And I know that -- I heard about it, that Colonel Karremans personally also made several reports to the UNPROFOR Command to tell them that there was a troubling situation arising because of the lack of personnel and the lack of supplies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, there is a suggestion in your question as -- that demilitarisation was the task of UNPROFOR, I take it. Is that what you find in the agreement? If so, then I better understand your question. Whether your interpretation is right or wrong but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question was related to the testimony of the witness when he was talking about when you want to demilitarise. I'm asking whether any of that was communicated upwards to see whether they were discussing whether, in fact, demilitarisation was a task that had been tasked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have the perception of the witness. Perhaps we should ask him. Was it, Witness, your task to demilitarise the area or were the parties to demilitarise it? What, in your view, was the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our objective was to uphold the demilitarised zone. And whenever we would get into contact with weapons or see that Muslim forces would carry weapons, we -- we had the -- it was part of the mission that we would try to take those weapons in. But due to the fact that we had so little personnel, there was no separate activity other than asking the Muslim forces to hand over their weapons and also abiding the agreement that the area should be demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should -- should they have been there at all under the existing regime? Should there have been any military presence of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was not the -- that -- that was not the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer is a bit ambiguous. Was it the agreement that they should not be there or was it not the agreement that they -- Could you please ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They should not be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They should not be there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They should not be there. No military activities from the Muslim forces should be there. But they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And to that extent -- do you -- demilitarisation, when you're talking about it, do you mean to remove or get rid of any military presence and activity; or do you understand it to be to seize weapons or -- what's your understanding of what demilitarisation means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically the -- the moments we would see that Muslim forces had weapons was because we were being shot during our patrols in the -- in the area. So in -- in such -- in such a way, and in those situations, it's not a discussion or asking the Muslim soldier that's shooting you to hand over his weapon. So we could see sometimes that Muslim men were carrying weapons, and -- but most of the time we only would know it because they were shooting at us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you then tell them that they shouldn't be there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had several contacts with Muslim commanders in the area which I was responsible for, which was the northeastern part of the enclave and also had the observation post Quebec and Romeo in that area. And of course, I spoke with those Muslim commanders that they shouldn't be there carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But should they be there at all? I'm talking about military presence and military activity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's -- it's difficult to make a clear separation between the refugees and -- and the population that was in the enclave and say, Okay, those were refugees and civilians, and those men are soldiers. Because it was not as -- as organised as we -- as we were. So it's -- it's difficult to say that -- we could -- we could speak to one of the men in -- in a village and he would be a civilian and dressed in civilian clothes, and maybe an hour later he would go up with a weapon, take up a weapon, and then maybe shoot at us or at the Serb forces. So it was not clear to see, well, this is the military presence and these are the civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And you had asked me if it was part of the agreement. P23, the 8 May 1993 agreement signed by General Mladic, General Halilovic and by General Morillon on behalf of UNPROFOR, at part 1, Article 5, does have in the agreement the description of the role of UNPROFOR in relation to enforcing or controlling, I should say, the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And who -- from whom were weapons to be seized in Article 5, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Any weapons coming in and any persons, it says, in Serbian. [Interpretation] "... Any of the soldiers would not be allowed to enter or be in the excluded zone."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you said something about the task of UNPROFOR. This is an obligation for soldiers, isn't it? And you were referring to paragraph 5. Let me have the text with it for a second. Perhaps we could have it on our screen --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... English version. It's on page 2 of P23 in the English, Your Honour. It says UNPROFOR shall control the demilitarised zone and then it goes to detail all these things that I have been reading to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And from whom were the weapons to be seized?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Any armed persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any armed persons. Let me check. One second, please. "Non-combatants who are in or who are willing to enter the demilitarised zone, except members of UNPROFOR, are not permitted to have in their possession any weapon, ammunition, or explosives. Weapons, ammunition, and explosives in their possession shall be seized by UNPROFOR." Here that is about non-combatants. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Next line, Your Honour. "Combatants will not be allowed to enter or be in the demilitarised zone."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think there's no disagreement that -- but I'm looking at the Prosecution as well, that that's what combatants shouldn't do. We are also talking about seizure of weapons. Article 5, the last paragraph, gives no specific task, it seems, to UNPROFOR. But I'm happy to find any other provision where the UNPROFOR tasks, as we find in the fourth paragraph of Article 5, are set out in further detail. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you had testified about some difficulties in getting DutchBat personnel back from leave that caused the numbers in the enclave to dip. Am I correct that even prior to those individuals leaving, the zone still had not been -- still was not demilitarised? That is to say, the personnel that were originally deployed, whatever that number was, I presume it was more than 300, would not have been sufficient to demilitarise an area of the size of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the Dutch battalion have -- or UNPROFOR, to your knowledge, have any figures or estimates as to the strength of the armed Bosnian Muslim contingent in the Srebrenica enclave in 1995?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any recollection of that. Maybe there were some estimates during that time, but I don't have any recollection of that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough. Now, was a problem that you were experiencing -- you indicated oftentimes that you were -- UNPROFOR would be fired upon by Bosnian Muslims. Would it also be the case that, whether fired upon or not, when you saw Bosnian Muslims armed with weapons and when you tried to disarm them, they would run away and disappear into the terrain since they knew it better?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was it also correct that you did not have the capability of doing all the patrolling that had been envisioned, such that you did not have an ability to exert control over the entirety of the terrain that was within the zone of responsibility of your duties, that northern part of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you about an individual named Nasir Sabanovic. If you can tell me who he was in 1995, his position, and if you had occasion to encounter this individual?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nasir Sabanovic was a military commander, Bosnian Muslim commander, in the -- in the area of my responsibility. And most of the time when I was staying at OP Quebec, I would have conversations with him about his activities and what he thought of the activities of the Serb forces on -- on the other side of the -- outside of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Van Duijn, there's no need to switch off your microphone any further because the technical problems have been resolved and the rumble is gone. So that you can concentrate on the questions and on your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That assists me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, would there be occasions when Mr. Sabanovic or other Bosnian Muslim military leaders would be meeting with yourself or with your superiors in the Dutch battalion and in the course of those meetings would be armed with side-arms?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some occasions, Nasir Sabanovic would have side-arms with him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did anyone on the part of the UNPROFOR Dutch battalion ever tell Mr. Sabanovic that he should not be armed or try to disarm him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meetings I had with him, because he did not have meetings with my superiors, meetings I had with him, I told him that he should not carry a weapon, but I did not try to disarm him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, same follow-up question. Did you tell him that he should not be in the enclave. You talk about him as a military commander of the Muslim forces. Earlier we established that they shouldn't be there. You explained what difficulties you would have to define exactly who would be a -- a soldier and who would be a non-combatant. But for Mr. Sabanovic, there could hardly be any doubt as to his military status. First, do you agree with that; and, second, was he ever told that he shouldn't be there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- I do not agree with that. Because every time I spoke with Nasir Sabanovic he would always tell me that he did not want to be in that situation. And also, if I remember correctly, every time I had a conversation with him, he was always dressed in civilian clothes, never in -- in -- never in uniform. And he would explain to me that he was, due to the situation, forced to -- to take up arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you describe him yourself as a military commander. Are you saying there should be no military presence? You explained your difficulties and whatever he may have been dressed in, isn't it true that you considered him to be a military leader? And under the demilitarisation agreement, no military leader should be there, no military presence at all should be there. Did you ever tell him? And you said he didn't want to be in that situation. Does that change anything under the terms of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the difficulty there is to -- to see if he was a military commander as I saw him, because he was the only commander in the area that I could speak to, I think that one -- in one of the occasions I had a conversation with him, he told me that he saw himself as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just ... I'm just reading your: "Nasir Sabanovic was a military commander, Bosnian Muslim commander, in the area of my responsibility. And most of the time when I was staying at OP Quebec, I would have conversations with him about his activities and what he thought of the activities of the Serb forces on the other side of the enclave." Whether he saw himself as a civilian, if someone arrives with a tank and says, I'm a civilian, you describe him as a military commander. If you say, Perhaps I should have told him, that's -- that's fine, but it seems that you are -- in your answers, you are making him a quasi civilian where you started by saying that you discussed his activities and you mentioned him a military commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I can imagine that you say, well, perhaps he should have acted differently. My question simply was: Did you ever tell him that military commanders should not be there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never told him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically I was -- I was glad that I had some sort of a chain of command when it came to the Muslim soldiers in that area. Because I could also speak to him about shootings that would happen from inside the enclave on our UN forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it had certain advantages for you to keep the status quo, as it was, including the military presence. Is that -- I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the course of your interactions and discussions with Mr. Nasir Sabanovic was he, in fact, rather candid about his participation in combat and sabotage activities, such as military activities including going outside the enclave, setting mines and destroying -- destroying Serb military assets?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was very candid about that. And yes, that's true. He told me that he would go on patrol outside of the enclave and, as you described, placing mines, actually performing raids outside of the enclave, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you any stories about his -- about himself or -- or -- or Muslim soldiers going out and burning down Serb villages surrounding Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if he actually spoke about burning down villages, but he spoke about performing raids and placing mines and -- and those kinds of -- and those kinds of activities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now let me take a step back away from Mr. Sabanovic and ask you a more general question. Did you ever have occasion to find out about or hear stories about incidents where Muslim soldiers going out from the Srebrenica enclave burned down Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard stories about that, yes, in other areas that were not under my responsibility but in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the question I have for you is you say you heard stories. Can you enlighten us from what types of sources you heard about these stories happening where Bosnian Muslim fighters from within Srebrenica went outside the enclave and burnt down Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From other commanders, like myself, UN commanders, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm a bit puzzled by one of the previous answers. The question was whether you ever found out about or hear stories about Muslim soldiers going out from the Srebrenica enclave burning down Serb villages. Your answer was: "I've heard stories about that, yes, in other areas that were not under my responsibility but in the enclave." Did you want to say that you heard it in the enclave or that it happened in the enclave? Because the question was about going out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did not happen in the enclave. I heard it from other commanders, colleagues of mine from DutchBat, that were responsible for other areas and that had seen from their observation posts or patrols or from Muslim commanders in that area that they would leave the enclave and enter the Serb area and then burn down villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you have occasion to talk with the Serb soldiers on the other side of the dividing line, and were they friendly and open in their discussions with you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to my other OP, Romeo, there was a bunker, a Serb bunker, just outside the enclave border, and we had discussions, sometimes were friendly, sometimes less friendly, but we had open communications with them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you something slightly different in relation to demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to do so, I'd like to call up a document, 65 ter number 1D900 in e-court. And, first of all, if we can have the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, I don't know, sir, if you'd like to have it in Dutch or in English, but I'd like to see if you can recognise this document before we go into its contents. So perhaps the original Dutch, first page?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: English or Dutch is fine by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine then.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the -- the first page of my debriefing, which took part in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And would that be the debriefing with the Dutch Royal Army in September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to have page 8 in English. And it is page 7 in the B/C/S, and if we need it, it's page 8 in the Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it is the first full paragraph at the top of the page in English, and, sir, if would you follow along with me, I have some questions relating to this debriefing document. And it begins as follows: "After OP E was taken, the Muslims improved many of their positions. They also dug many more trenches. More foxholes were also added. During their patrols, the Muslim would say not allow them into Zanik anymore. It was unclear why. The Kvarac height, 789, was filled with Muslim fighters at the time. "During this period, the presence of the Serbs was so threatening that a blind eye was turned to the Muslims' arms. "In his sector, no weapons were taken from Muslims at this time. It was indicated by the battalion that they should turn a blind eye to this under the guise of the right to self-defence. This went on while many Muslims were walking around with weapons. During his meetings with the UN, Nasir always had a pistol with him. The Muslims generally kept these weapons out of sight when they were in the vicinity of the OPs. The UN personnel had tried to disarm the Muslims from the start. However, this was not often successful because the Muslims always ran away." And, first, the formalities, sir, can you confirm if what is stated here and what I have read into the record is truthful and accurate as to the matters that are contained therein, such that you would testify the same if asked to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's truthful and accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to ask you a bit more about this. Here it is recorded, and the word that is used in the English is that it was "indicated" by the battalion. Who within the Dutch battalion communicated to you this position that your personnel should turn a blind eye to the Bosnian Muslim weapons?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember at the time I was at OP Quebec, and all the communications and directives then at that time came through my company commander, Captain Mathijssen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you have used the term "communications and directives." Did you consider this communication to turn a blind eye to the Bosnian Muslim weapons to be a directive from your superior officers within the battalion?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you also directed or instructed by anyone in the battalion, any superior officer, to keep quiet about such a directive?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now while we already have this document on the screen I'd like to touch on another part which is on the same page in the English and Dutch but will be on the next page in the Serbian version about a related but different topic. And it is in the middle of the page right after the -- the sentence that said: "The Muslims also had good weapons such as fairly new Kalashnikovs."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to have you follow along, sir, and it begins as follows: "The Serbs told stories about American air-drops and UN helicopters with supplies. He had seen lights in the dark, which could have come from a helicopter. After this, the battalion had asked for the AWACS to make a pass, but these turned out to be 'coincidently not available.' This incident was concurrent with the info from the Serbs that there had been American air-drops. Patrols also later found the remains of American emergency rations and tin cans, et cetera." First of all, sir, I have to ask you, if you would be the "he" in this selection who saw lights in the dark, which could have come from a helicopter?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "he" refers to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then I have to ask you if the information that I have just read out from this debriefing report is truthful and accurate, such that you would testify today if asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's truthful and accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you explain for us in some detail what happened with the AWACS? And perhaps in your answer could you explain for everyone what an AWACS is.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: An AWACS aeroplane is, to describe it easily, sort of a radar equipment that when it flies over a certain area, it then can detect any activity in the air. Other planes or helicopters that are active and flying there. So that's why we also requested, we had heard that -- that sometimes there was an AWACS plane available to us. And, at that time, we had requested, because in the days before these incidents, we sometimes saw during the night some lights in the -- in the skies. Of course, it was dark, so you could see the lights. And sometimes also heard some helicopter rotor blade noise. So that made us request when we heard those noises and saw those lights again to request an AWACS aeroplane if it was in the neighbourhood, but that did not happen, at least as I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, for the record, these AWACS radar planes that had been discussing, what country or what air force was operating the AWACS planes over head, as per your understanding?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really sure which country had those planes at that time. I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you at least recall that they would have been a NATO member nation or was it -- or was there some other air alliance flying over the territory? Again, if you know. If you don't, that's --

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever author any report on this incident apart from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One seconds. Could you also please slow down also for the transcription.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself author any report on this incident apart from mentioning it in, I believe, all the debriefings that you had following your deployment?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe only the reports in the mission area. But I don't know if that was done on paper or just through radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And do you have any recollection -- first of all, we've been -- we've been talking about the one incident where an AWACS plane was requested and you were told it was not available, but I get from your discussion that perhaps the visual and audio clues to the existence of helicopters flying in occurred on several occasions, am I correct, or is it just one occasion?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were multiple occasions. I can't recollect how many in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough. Now, these emergency rations that you report that patrols found, would those patrols have been -- strike that. Would those rations have been the types of things that normally could be seen via humanitarian aid or were they of a military nature?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were of a military nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Knowing the situation in Srebrenica during the summer of 1995, do you believe that such emergency rations of a military nature could have come by any other means apart from being brought in from the outside in some form?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they must have been brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, one more thing from this document on this page before I move on. And it is the second-to-last paragraph from the bottom in the English version. And, again, I will read it for you and then ask you some questions. It reads as follows: "There were also two members of the British SAS, Jim and Dave, inside the enclave, which the battalion had attached to 108. He did not know what the orders of these SAS members inside the enclave were. He had heard from Lieutenant Caris that these SAS men served as liaison officers of sorts for General Smith and were in direct contact with him. DutchBat viewed them rather as busybodies inside the unit." Now, first of all, where it says that: "He did not know what the orders of the SAS members inside the enclave were," is that, again, you, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the sentence: "He had heard from Lieutenant Caris that these SAS men served as liaison officers of sorts for General Smith and were in direct contact with him." Am I correct that the first "he" is you, that is, you heard from Lieutenant Caris, and the last "him" would be General Smith?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now with these clarifications, do you confirm that this selection that I have read to you is truthful and accurate as to the facts contained therein?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's truthful and accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I inquire as to what the reference to 108 stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. I'm sorry. Then the next question of Mr. Ivetic is what the reference to 108 stands for? Could you answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 108 was the number of the commando and reconnaissance unit that was part of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, just one item of clarification. I believe that in your answer you did not add -- this was a commando unit of the Royal Dutch Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did 108 have the same mission as the remainder of the Dutch battalion?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did 108 report according to the same chain of command as the Dutch battalion?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What was the numeric strength of that 108 Dutch commando unit?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one platoon, but I don't recall the exact strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if that 108 unit was acknowledged to the parties, that is, to the Serb and the Muslim side, as being present in Srebrenica or was its existence in any way obstrucated [sic] or concealed?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no concealed presence, and they acted as a special reconnaissance unit within the DutchBat, within DutchBat. So under the same set of rules and directives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock. Could you find a suitable moment within the next couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. How about one more question before we go to the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of assignments, if you know, did unit 108 perform whilst in the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- they also did patrols and special reconnaissance. But I don't have any information about the details of their assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I guess if we are at the time for the a break, we can have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd first invite the witness to follow the usher. And we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you're on your feet. I take it not to take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Could I raise a brief matter in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I will briefly read a short decision. The Chamber will deliver its decision on the Prosecution's urgent motion for testimony of Witness RM284 to be heard via video-conference link, a motion which was filed on the 5th of April of this year. Given the proposed date of testimony and the urgent nature of the motion, the Chamber exceptionally delivers its decision orally with written reasons to follow. After having considered the submissions of the parties, the Chamber finds that allowing the witness to testify via video-conference link is consistent with the interests of justice, and, therefore, the Chamber grants the motion. This concludes the Chamber's decision. Written reasons will follow in due course. We take a break and resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you're ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you a few more questions about this unit 108. Did unit 108 operate pursuant to blue orders or green orders, and in your answer, if you could please explain for persons who may not be familiar, what is the difference between a so-called blue order and a so-called green order?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first question, unit 108 also operated under the blue orders. So the normal activities of DutchBat. They were part of -- part of DutchBat. No question about that. The so-called green orders were more military-type activities, which I was confronted with on the evening of the 9th, where I, with two APCs during the night went under the cover the darkness, although we were with white UN APCs, we tried to cover our activities, so in a more green or military type of way, to go over to the south of the enclave to start working at the blocking positions. Regarding 108, they followed the activities of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at 1D900 again. And this time if we can have page 11 in the English and page 10 of the B/C/S. And if anyone is following, it's also page 11 in the Dutch I have confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think that this selection is in relation to the time-period that you describe between the 9th and 10th of July, at the blocking position, but I'll wait to present it to you and get your response.
