It is the last full paragraph, or the beginning of the last full paragraph on the page in the English and reads as follows: "The forward air controllers came running back and jumped into the waiting YPR and quickly attached themselves to the back of the convoy. He waited a moment in his YPR and then withdrew step by step." Now, first of all, sir, the "he" in this selection, would that again be a reference to yourself?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with that additional information, sir, can you confirm that the facts as recited here in this selection are truthful and accurate, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're truthful and accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, first of all, YPR, do you understand that to be an acronym, perhaps transliterated from the original Dutch, to be the armoured personnel carriers that you had mentioned, the APCs?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The YPR is the Dutch term for the type of APC we used there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And these persons that you have identified as the forward air controllers, first of all, who were they? Were they in fact persons from unit 108?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were part of 108, combined with the British SAS soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I accurate that incident occurred during the time-period that you're talking about, between the 9th and 10th of July, when you withdrew your original position to establish at the blocking point which was -- I believe point 02 is the designation?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm correct it was the 11th of July, and I was withdrawing from the original location of my blocking position, south of the town towards the compound of the Bravo Company which was in Srebrenica town, and just before I entered from the southern area to the compound in Srebrenica, the forward air controllers came back from their mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you say that the forward air controllers came back from their mission. Was it your understanding that the mission that they had just been performing was acting as spotters calling down NATO close air support air strikes against Serb targets?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew that. Of course, we already had asked for air support, and this was the only incident we -- we actually got close air support. And forward air controlling, means, in another word spotting for the plane that provided us with close air support. And I, of course, could see the effect because also the anti-aircraft guns of the Serbs were shooting at the planes that provided the close air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now let me ask you in relation to what we talked about earlier, would these activities of the forward air controllers calling down the military air strikes against Serb positions would those be qualified as green orders, that is, military orders, or blue orders, peacekeeping orders?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even as part of the blue orders, we were -- we had the possibility to call in air support. But, in fact, from the evening of the 9th on, basically every order that was given to DutchBat personnel was a green order, more or less of a green character, because we had to do those orders and do those missions with white APCs, with blue helmets, and so basically a real green execution of those orders was not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think this witness has explained that he makes a distinction between air strikes and close air support. In his answers I hear always close air support. In your questions you continue to talk about air strikes. That might create confusion at a later stage. So would you please -- may I invite you to avoid that confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And perhaps so that we are clear, could you, sir, tell us what is your understanding of the distinction between air strikes and close air support, the term that you have used?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason why I always speak about close air support is because that was part of our mandate, and close air support is, in fact, pin-pointed support that you get from -- from an aeroplane to really at one location try to -- to help the troops on the ground. Air strikes, as the Judge mentioned, has a different character, is more massive and not pin-pointed to one location or co-ordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, sir. I would like to now again turn to your Rule 92 ter testimony, which is Exhibit P1154.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would like to turn to the -- I believe it's the eighth page of the same, which is transcript page -- page 2261. Actually, I think it's the ninth page in the -- 2261. That's the page. 6-1. Back -- back to the page we had. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention, sir, to lines 13 through 16 of this document, here, you are talking about and describing that the observation posts tried to trade with the local population to be in better shape diet-wise with food. Did you have occasion to hear about or eye-witness the operation of a black market on the part of the armed BiH forces or the Armija BiH forces in the enclave selling humanitarian aid that had been delivered to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. If we could, we can see what -- what we are using as the 92 ter statement where we used adjudicated facts to delete the record. If it would be possible that we could use the actual full record so when the witness is reading it, he will have a chance because it -- right to the point that he gets, we have an adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to put to the witness the answers he gave, then, of course, it's not of great help, Mr. Ivetic, that he reads adjudicated fact number so-and-so. So, therefore, if there's any way to produce the original version of the transcript, that certainly would help. Do you have it available for yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not in e-court, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But I do believe my question goes beyond what is here. I was just using this as a starting point. I mean, I'm asking about the black market. He is not talking about that here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that's not -- Mr. McCloskey, of course, I could check immediately now all the adjudicated facts. Let's proceed. If Mr. Ivetic asks his question if at any point in time you consider it necessary for the witness to be informed about what is now not visible in this transcript, please get on your feet again. You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you have occasion to hear about or eye-witness the operation of a black market on the part of the Armija BiH forces in the enclave selling humanitarian aid that had been delivered to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about -- when I was in the enclave, I heard about certain elements, and I don't know if they were part of BiH forces. Certain elements using and selling humanitarian aid elements to -- to refugees. You can think about coffee and sugar that was brought into the -- to the enclave. So I -- I heard about it, and I've never been there, as far as I recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge or eye-witness incidents where Armija BiH members in the enclave offered DutchBat personnel the opportunity to participate in such illicit activities such as black marketeering?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard stories about that. I've never eye-witnessed it or been a part of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to see or hear about the Armija BiH forces in Srebrenica attempting to offer prostitution to the members of the DutchBat battalion at the observation posts?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the same time I also heard about those stories. And just a clarification to both questions. For me, it was not clear that BiH forces were behind those -- those attempts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask for clarification. With the caveat that you don't know whether they were BiH forces, were the -- were the, let's say, individuals or parties that were making such offers situated from within the enclave itself?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was true, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have occasion to witness or hear about the persons within the Srebrenica enclave engaging in internal fighting and assassinations to settle scores relating to the control of the black market?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard about that. That -- I've heard stories about settling scores amongst themselves but not what the topics were that they were struggling about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I want to step away from this black market scenario and talk to something a little bit closer to home. Within a -- and ... and if any of this needs to be, you believe, in private session, please let me know. But within a few weeks of your deployment to Srebrenica, was there an unsettling experience that you encountered relative to persons back in the Netherlands? And, again, if you feel that we need to go into private session, I will be more than happy to oblige the request.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That will not be necessary, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you recall the incident I'm talking about where your home address in the Netherlands received some letter from a brother of one of the Muslim commanders in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to 1D900, debriefing report that we've been dealing with. And I think it's page 2 of both of the English and the Dutch, and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that is the most succinct summary of the incident that I'd like to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, it's page 2 in the Dutch and the English. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it is the last paragraph on the page, sir, and if you would follow along: "In February, his girlfriend had received a letter from a Yugoslav who lived in Amsterdam. This turned out to be the brother of Ibro Smajic. A letter was included with the words, 'Your boyfriend knows about it and the money is on the way,' accompanied by a letter in Serbo-Croat. He had informed OWI? Rave of this. Later an envelope did arrive containing 800 German marks. He had no idea how the Yugoslavs had found out his address. Rave believed that the OP C of the 12th Sergeant 1st Class Hagenbeek may have done this because he was often in contact with Ibro Smajic. When he left, Hagenbeek had given Ibro Smajic sports shoes and a jogging outfit. He knew that someone else had also experienced something similar." First of all, sir, does this passage truthfully and accurately depict the facts pertaining to this incident that we've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's truthful and accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the individual identified as Rave that had the question marks into it who you told about this incident and who suspected one of your colleagues may have assisted the Bosnian Muslim commander to contact persons back in the Netherlands, who was this individual named Rave or Rave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- OWI stands for his rank, is an abbreviation for the Dutch rank opperwachtmeester. And the name is Bert Rave, and I think you know him because he was the former witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I presume although the letter said your brother [sic] knows about it, I presume you did not know, in fact, anything about why this letter or the money had been sent; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's accurate. I did not know how they found out my address, and I did not know about money or some -- something else that was -- there were some gestures in it and also a letter in Serbo-Croat which we had translated. But I knew nothing of the -- of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in this selection the last sentence says: "He knew that someone else had also experienced something similar." Relating to, I guess, a colleague giving information to the Bosnian Muslims that was of a sensitive personal nature. Is the "he" that knew that others had experienced this talking about you or about Mr. Rave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The "he" refers to me. As I read it now, I have no recollection of another person that had experienced something similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And now, I'd like to ask you about some related topics and I think the most efficient way is to present to you a list of your responses to questions from the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So in e-court I would ask for 65 ter number 1D898 to be brought up and ask for page 6 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we will begin at line 2 from the top and, please, if you can, follow along, sir, and I will have questions at the end: "Q. And was there a suspicion that internal mail was being interfered with by the local population? "A. Yeah, there were more suspicions of our information or personal information was also known to local Muslim military commanders. "Q. And I think also there was a case of the main switchboard at Bravo Company being connected to by a member of the local population? "A. Yeah. That's what I heard about, yes. "Q. You've been asked one or two questions about this already but I'd like to develop the theme. It became apparent to you during the course of your time there that there were other agencies at work in and around the enclave, didn't it? By which I mean military agencies. "A. Yes, that's true. "Q. You were asked yesterday about the presence of the British SAS in the enclave. They were not part of the mission, were they? "A. I believe they had their own mission but they were put with us on our compound. "Q. And you didn't know whether their objectives were consistent with yours or wholly inconsistent with yours. "A. I have no information about that. "Q. I think you also became aware that there were American military personnel operating in the area of the enclave. "A. I don't have any information about that as well. The only thing that we noticed, that we found some American rations when we did our patrols." Now, first of all, sir, do you confirm that the text I've just read is both truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's truthful and accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And let's start from the back end. The incident with the American rations, would that be the incident we discussed earlier where we were talking about military emergency food rations?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's the same incident. Speaking about the same rations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah. And when you testified in this section that it became apparent to you that were other military agencies at work in and around the enclave, were you merely making reference to the supplying of the force -- the Armija BiH forces or did you mean that you felt that foreign agencies had a physical presence inside of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I was referring to was the activities of the SAS and not about supplying the BiH forces or other foreign agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, I want to focus during the time-period the -- of the 9th, 10th, and, I guess, also the 11th of July, at the blocking position. And you discuss this in some detail in your Rule 92 ter testimony, beginning at page 11 and onwards, and at page 15 of P1154, which should correlate to transcript page 2268 of that 92 ter transcript. At the top of the page at line 1 there's a reference that the Muslim soldiers were gone. And I think that this is a reference relating to a discussion of the southern part of Srebrenica that is on the page prior. And I want to ask you: According to your knowledge, where had these Muslim soldiers been situated that were now gone at the time of -- of the events that are transpiring at this page of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please read the previous page --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely --

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because it puts things more in perspective, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn back and zoom in on the second half of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. It's clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now these Muslim soldiers that you said were gone, could you help orient us as to where these Muslim soldiers had been situated that were now gone.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the -- the side of the blocking positions where I was then, south of the town. And we stayed there until the refugees, as is stated in the previous page, the refugees had time to move on northwards to where the Potocari base was -- was located. And there was a period of time during the night and the morning in which there still were Muslim soldiers there, taking -- also taking a position near our locations of the blocking position. And when I'm referring to at the top of this page I see before me now is that at one time also the Muslim soldiers were retreating, were gone, and from the point I was standing, I could see that they were -- also were going northwards in the same direction as the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: These Muslim soldiers that you have now more specifically defined for us, did you have any kind of information or estimate about their numeric strength if you recall?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the direct vicinity of my APC, there were varying in strength, somewhere between sometimes 5, sometimes 10, sometimes 20, but that must be the maximum amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can move forwards in the transcript a bit, I believe it's the 18th page of your Rule 92 ter transcript that we have in e-court right now. And it should be transcript page 2271 of the underlying case's transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, may I ask one --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- question. You said they were gone. They -- they moved in the same direction. Do you remember what -- were they carrying any arms and, if so, what kind of arms? And how did they move? Did they have any vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They moved on foot. And the thing they had with them in my direct vicinity were one heavy machine-gun placed on a tripod and other hand fire-arms, pistols and -- and on one occasion also a rocket-launcher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rifles, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I see we now have the page that I was asking for on the screen. If we could move it down so that lines 17 to 22 are visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's where I'd like to ask you. Here, sir, at lines 17 to 22 of the 18th page of P1154, you state that you saw some Muslim men at this point going towards Susnjari, and I don't want to misquote you so let me actually read in full the answer: "A. In fact that was still when we were located at 0.02, we saw a big group of men going towards Susnjari, or leaving from 0.02 towards OP Mike, so the other direction, and we could see them leaving -- carrying small-calibre weapons with them. Men of all sorts of age, even young boys and old men with them. Not all of them were armed, but they were all men and going in that direction." And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you wanted to read in order to be accurate. You read, "or" where the text says "so." Second line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the first question I have for you is: Is this the group of Muslim soldiers that we've been discussing up until this point that were gone on the morning of the 11th? Or is it a different group?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the group on the morning of the 11th was much smaller. This was a big group. It could be that the soldiers I had seen on the morning of the 11th and on the 10th and for the 9th, for what it's worth, could be part of that big group that I saw on the -- on the 11th near .02 leaving for Susnjari. But I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now focussing on this group that you've identified here as a big group heading towards Susnjari, can you qualify for us what does "big" mean in as specific terms as you are able to do?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there must have been hundreds of men and young boys and older men in that group. There were really actually part of a sort of column walking in the direction of Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say they were -- they were carrying smaller -- smaller calibre weapons with them or that some of them were, I should say, are we talking about the same types of weapons, pistols, rifles, perhaps machine-guns, perhaps RPGs?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only weapons I saw there were only small-calibre rifles, so no heavy machine-guns or RPGs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And a clarification in the answer you just gave. Did you say small-calibre weapons or small-calibre rifles?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Small-calibre weapons, meaning pistols and rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now this group, this large group, am I correct that at some point in time they kept going in a certain direction and coming back repeated times? Is this the group that did that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them leaving from .02 in a western direction and never saw them coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page of your Rule 92 ter testimony. That would be the 19th page in e-court. And if we could focus on lines 16 through 24. And here, sir, you are talking about -- at the morning getting word, basically a message that the Serb forces had taken over the enclave and that your assignment was to put away your weapons and basically to only give humanitarian aid thereafter? And the question I have for you, first of all, is if you can tell us ... can you tell us prior to this point, had your orders been primarily of a green nature, that is to say, a military nature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get a date? It's not clear from the record what date we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall what date you received this? Would it have been the 11th or the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the 12th of July, the first day the transports started.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And would you agree that the orders you had been receiving prior to this order from your superiors had been of a -- had been tending towards a green designation, whereas this order was of a purely blue designation?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the evening on the 9th, I was assigned with, as we call it, the green order, to take up the blocking position and try to stop or at least try to prevent the -- the movement of the Serb forces, the advancement of the Serb forces northwards so that the refugees had time to move up to the Potocari area. And that green order lasted until this order where we should put away our weapons, but that actually went further than the blue assignment we had from the beginning of the mission. Because, as part of the blue assignment, the normal mission which DutchBat had also contained rules of engagement, the possibility to ask for close air support, so that was a larger assignment that we had from that moment on. From that moment on, the only thing we could do was provide humanitarian aid which was smaller than the mission we had before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the orders that were of a mixed green and blue variety prior, did you at any time receive orders to co-ordinate with the Bosnian Muslim soldiers your actions, shooting at the Bosnian Serb forces that were advancing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, before we continue, you said: "In relation to the orders that were of a mixed green and blue variety prior ..." Now, the witness may correct me, I understood that the witness considered the orders before the 9th, which included the broader mission, that would include -- rules of engagement, possibility to ask for close-air support, you consider those still blue orders. So if I understood that well, then your mixed green/blue orders is a bit confusing, Mr. Ivetic, unless you point at which orders you are exactly referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, at transcript page 63, number 4, the witness started off his answer by saying: "From the evening on the 9th, I was assigned with, as we call it, the green order," so the orders are both green and blue in that time-period. I'm asking in that time-period are any of them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's make a distinction between mission and order. I did understand that an order was issued on the 9th, which tended to not openly operate and therefore behave more in a military way. That order you called a green order, I did understand that the orders you received before that date were blue orders, unless I have misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you're correct. In my mind, there was no mixing of orders until the 9th. From the 6th of January until the 9th of July, we were part of a blue mission with blue activities in it. From the 9th of July, the evening of the 9th, my activities were more green, more military, more trying to be covert, and, of course, also with combat activities, firing and being fired upon. So and that lasted until the -- the morning of the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those -- in this understanding of the testimony, Mr. Ivetic, it's a bit unclear to what you refer as the mixed blue/green orders and let's make a distinction between orders and mission. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will make it very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The orders that you received between the 9th and the 12th of July, did any of those orders include co-ordinating your combat actions against the Serb forces with the Bosnian Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall if I received orders, but looking at my own blocking position and the activities of Muslim forces there, I co-ordinated with them as well as we could to at least not shoot each other from that side on. This -- so I don't know if I received any orders through the chain of command but I did that on site, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to fast-forward a bit and focus on the time-period when you arrived at the UN compound in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I -- Your Honour, may I elaborate a little bit on the situation there just to show how difficult the situation was. Because at one period of time, we tried to co-ordinate with the soldiers that were there, the Muslim soldiers that were there, but with the changing -- I already spoke about the changing in numbers and the changing of persons. So a few hours later, I found myself in a position where a Muslim soldier had taken a position with a rocket-launcher in front of my APC and they told me that that was because the Muslim forces wanted to prevent us from leaving that location. So it was very difficult to co-ordinate with the Muslim forces that were present there because they were constantly changing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And during that time-period, sir, when the RPG was at your APC, and I can't remember if it was one or two RPGs, but at that time were you also threatened by the Bosnian Muslim forces that they would fire upon you if, in fact, there were not -- more close air support or strikes against the Bosnian Muslim forces? Was that communicated to you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that was any relation to the close air support. It was just, as I remember, our taking up the blocking position and possibly leaving the blocking position. And it clarifies also maybe the statement made before that when the Muslim soldiers left that location, I was free to operate and take up another position to -- a new blocking position at another location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that, sir. Now, I'd like to again return to the time-period when you arrived at the UN compound. And, first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I ask one question. Do I understand your answer well that when the Muslim forces were still there and when they were using an RPG against you, that you did not feel free to move your position as you wished to do, and only be free to do that after they had left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we could focus on the time-period when you arrived at the UN compound at Potocari. And I'd like to first direct you to the 12th of July. Am I correct that at some point in time, the Serb army fighters left and were replaced by Serb police personnel?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that I did not arrive at the UN compound. That was later that evening. But I was near the vicinity between the compound and .02, so south of the -- of the compound. So not at the UN compound. But at one point at time, Serb police personnel, as they identified themselves, also came to that location, yes. I don't know if they were replaced, but at one point in time Serb police personnel also entered the location that I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to now turn to 1D897 which is again an expansion of the Popovic transcript. And page 30 of the same in e-court, which should correlate to transcript page 2341 of that trial's transcript record. And if we can focus on the second half of the page, beginning with line 14 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I'd like to again use the same procedure of presenting this to you and then asking you for some follow-up or clarification if it is accurate, first. Beginning at 14: "When you continued with your testimony yesterday, and this is on page 53 of the transcript, lines 9 to 12, you said that you were in contact with Major Franken and that you heard from him that he also was aware of the fact that the refugees would be transported and that's when it practically became clear to you that this would actually happen. Is that correct? "A. Yes. In my contacts with Major Franken, he confirmed that he had also heard, in talks, that this was the case and that the refugees were supposed to be transported out of the enclave. "Q. So Major Franken already knew this when you called him. Is this correct? "A. Yes. This is correct. Basically he was surprised that it was already happening. "Q. So from this, from your reply, can we conclude that the agreement on the evacuation of the refugees was achieved at a much higher level than your level and the level of Captain Mane, who were actually there at the actual location? "A. I don't know if there was any agreement of the sort. What was clear that not only on my level but also on a higher level, there were talks about the evacuation of the refugees." And now, sir, can you confirm if you stand by the -- this selection of your testimony as being truthful and accurate as to the facts contained therein.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're truthful and accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to any talks or meetings at a higher level, did you have any actual knowledge that you came to, perhaps at this time or later, or would you have to defer to others on that -- on that topic?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have that at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I will limit my questions to what you knew or heard. And first of all, did any of your superiors, including Major Franken, ever tell you that the evacuations of the population out of the enclave was something that was considered a bad thing and that should -- that such acts should be prevented?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that I heard every -- anything from Major Franken about this, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 69 of this same transcript in e-court. That ought to be page 2380 of the underlying transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could just look at lines 18 through 19 -- 18 through 25, I apologise, and I will ask you as follows. The quoted part begins: "Q. Is it right to say that the quick evacuation of the people from Potocari was the only solution for the population? "A. At that time, when all the refugees were gathered at the factory sites, from that moment on, there was no other solution there than to evacuate them because, like I said before, there were -- there was a big possibility that epidemics would break out, people had no food, no water, and the temperature was very high. So from that moment on, there was no other solution, that's correct." Now, first of all, sir, do you stand by this portion of your prior testimony as being truthful and accurate, as to this particular topic?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's truthful and accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in addition, sir, is it a fact or is it accurate that refugees that had gathered there at Potocari, that, in fact, many of them expressed a desire and wished to leave the enclave for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that point it was also clear for them, having no home, no bed, no food, no water, that that was not the place to stay in now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, that the DutchBat had to form a human chain with their own personnel and later used two APCs to try and channel the crowds of people to try and keep them from stampeding and trampling each other trying to get onto the buses to get out of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, we formed a human chain across the road; that's correct. Also to try to calm the refugees. They were not only stampeding but also from -- from the heat, losing consciousness, falling down on the floor, and then there was the threat of trampling each other because of the chaotic situation. And later on, on the second day, we used four APCs, not two, to make some sort of a V-shaped form in which it was easier for us to guide the massive amount of refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if somewhere in the next two minutes you could find a moment for a break --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then you're invited to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think after this next question we can have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, on the second morning of the evacuation, that time-period when the Serbs had not yet arrived, and in the absence of the Serb personnel, would you say that the Bosnian Muslim refugees also exhibited eagerness and desire to leave Srebrenica and were not being forced onto the buses at that time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were eager to leave and I think also because at the time the Serb forces were not there, only the UN forces. I took the decision to already start the transports. And in my mind, I think also the refugees saw also the opportunity to keep their families together and board the buses and the trucks in a normal way without being pushed or kicked or brutalised in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break. You may follow the usher, Mr. Van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We do have another witness available. Right now I have no re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, how much time would you still need? After the break, there's another 40 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I -- I will either take the whole time or maybe even another ten, 15 minutes beyond that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could make an effort to see whether we could -- can conclude the evidence of that witness today, but the next witness doesn't have to remain stand by.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you would need, well, let's say, five or ten minutes more, we might even ask the indulgence of all those assisting us and see whether we could finish then, but certainly then before 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll see, Your Honours. I have, I believe, three short clips from the video that I'm not sure how long it will take to locate and play them. The clips themselves are only one or two minutes but -- or less than a minute, but I don't know how long it takes to get the clips up on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you given the numbers already?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We would be happy to assist, if possible. Mr. McCloskey is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He should be here at any moment, Your Honour, but we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to talk about the separations and -- and -- and matters that you've testified about in relation to the evacuations. And I'd like to first turn to P1154 and page 34 of the same, which again is your Rule 92 ter testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this should correlate to page 2387 of that transcript and I would ask for lines 6 to 13 to be focussed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here, sir, you are talking about the explanation that Mane gave you that they had a list of war criminals, Muslim war criminals, and were going to check each of the men to see if they were on that list. And am I correctly understanding from this testimony that you as a military person at first did not regard the separation of men from the refugees as anything other than what would be considered normal procedure under a time of armed conflict when one side takes over a territory from another?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Basically a normal procedure to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can turn to page -- well, we don't have to turn to the pages, but at pages 51 and 50 of this transcript, you talk about going over to the White House and finding some discarded passports. And at today's transcript page 12 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, there's no translation? I'm told it's fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Today's temporary transcript, page 12, line 4, you talked about, in addition to passports, finding also, I believe, ID documents in front of the White House. I'd like to re-visit your testimony from the Popovic case to see if I can refresh your recollection of what you actually found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can have 1D897 in e-court, and page 9 of the same in e-court. That should correlate to transcript 2320 of that day's transcript. And it's at the top, beginning from line 1. And I quote, sir: "Q. You also told us yesterday that once the refugees left Potocari on the 13th of July, 1995, they left behind quite a lot of their permanent items; among [sic] other things, you mentioned photographs, blankets. My question is whether other than photographs, blankets, you saw identification documents, identity cards, passports, driver's licences, weapons permits, and similar documents. "A. Passports I had seen were on the lawn of the 'White House' and if I'm not mistaken, the other photographs and blankets that I talked about yesterday were the personal items that were left behind in the refugee area. In the refugee area, I saw blankets, photographs. I didn't see specifics in the sense of passports in the refugee area. The passports I had seen were on the lawn of the White House. "Judge Agius: And identity cards and driver's licences, weapons permits. "The witness: No. I have not seen that, Your Honour. "Judge Agius: All right. Thank you." Sir, does this prior testimony from the Popovic proceedings refresh your recollection as to whether you found just passports in front of the White House and not identification documents?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That refreshes my memory. Thinking back at what I have found -- what I found in the lawn of the White House, I know for sure that there were passports there, and if I'm not mistaken, there were also other form of identity cards also in the -- in the lawn of the White House. But you must know that they were in Serbo-Croatian so they gave me the impression that there were also some sort of identity documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so are you now modifying the testimony that you gave in the Popovic case or are you confirming it? Because I'm now confused.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm confirming the testimony from the Popovic case, just making clear that where Judge Agius asked me about identity cards, drivers's licence and weapons permits, I think he was referring to the refugee area. And as I stated before, I hadn't seen any identity documents or other items than blankets or photographs in the refugee area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With regard to the White House, were the passports that you found all in one place or scattered about?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in an area -- basically the lawn of the White House which was 10 metres long and 4 or 5 metres wide and they were scattered on that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that you found a total of 20 to 25 passports which you collected and initially put in the pocket of your shorts?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The estimate sounds more or less correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did these appear to be the old Socialist Yugoslav passports or the new BiH passports? Or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the passports at that time were valid anymore?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that you cannot rule out the possibility that the Muslim men themselves discarded the passports?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know why they left their passports there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that in addition to the passports you found outside the White House, that you saw other refugees had discarded passports and other personal belongings at the bus station?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that at the bus station or the refugee area, as -- as we stated before, I haven't seen any passports there. Only other personal items, like blankets or photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, just for the Chamber better to understand your line of questioning, were you exploring the possibility that because the passports were not valid anymore, that those who may have left them on the lawn became aware of that and, for that reason, thought, They're not valid so therefore we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What, then, is it what you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness has identified what, I believe, Mane is said to have said to him about them not needing them anymore and that could be an alternative meaning of what those words mean. If a passport is no longer valid, one does not have a need for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the reason for those questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... line of questioning -- correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is clear to the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, that the original statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor dated the 25th of October, 1995, had a reference in there that you had seen passports at the bus station which you then were presented with at the Popovic trial and which you stated you did not know how that had gotten into your ICTY statement? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no recollection of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For purposes of the record, since I did mention it, that's at page 2353 of the Popovic transcript. But in essence the witness says what he said today, that he does not remember seeing the passports at the bus station. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not evidence so the Chamber has no access to it. But if there's agreement on whether that is what the witness said, then, of course, the -- it's then hereby on the record. Mr. McCloskey, could you consider whether that's accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I will consider it. I don't recall immediately, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I can assist, it would be lines 1 through 23 of that page for Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did you have any knowledge as to the Bosnian civil system as it pertained to identity cards as the primary means of identification over passports?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any knowledge about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the words that you attributed to the Serb that you have called Mane as to these passports, I first want to ask you: Those words about the men not needing the passports anymore, were they spoken in English or through the assistance of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were spoken through the assistance of the interpreter, Miki that was always near to Mane and his interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you have the impression that Miki was not a professional interpreter but rather someone with a limited English knowledge thrust into that role?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the impression that Miki was a professional interpreter but he could speak excellent English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did Mane or anyone else on the part of the Serbs tell you not to take the passports or did they force you to return the passports?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not force me to return the passports or did they prevent me to take them, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And ... with regard to -- with regard to your interpretation of the nefarious meaning possible to Mane's words, would you agree that that is reached looking back now with the benefit of hindsight and because of the reports in the media of what is said to have later happened to men in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interpretation of the words of Mane had to be seen in the light of the -- the images that I already seen before I went on the mission, and you have to think about concentration camps, those images that were already in 1991 or 1992 on Dutch television as well. And we heard, of course, also in our training of that sort of atrocities happening. So in the course of the first day of the transports and the singling out of men, I had those images also in the back of my mind, and that is, of course, already a dark fate that will await men that are singled out. But you have to see my interpretation of the words of Mane made it even a darker fate for the -- the men that were singled out when he said that they would not need those passports anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And your discussion with Mane, again, related only to passports, not to identity documents?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke only about passports, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can have just briefly up in e-court number 1D00897 and page 51 of the same, which should relate to transcript page 2362.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here, sir, at lines 8 through 23, there's a rather lengthy discussion talking about the use of an identification card in lieu of a passport for identification purposes and the point that a person without a passport but with an identity card would be sufficiently identifiable especially under the law that was in place in Bosnia at the time. And I have looked, sir, while you have been talking, and I cannot find anywhere in the Popovic case where you at any point in time corrected anyone that was asking you questions about identity cards to claim that you also saw identity cards in front of the White House. Are you perhaps mistaken now, several years later, when you are raising the issue of identity cards having also been seen by you at the White House?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I'm mistaken, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to move to a related topic. At temporary transcript page 12, line 4, today you said that the White House was crammed. I want to try and establish how many men we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do this I would like to turn to page 1D -- pardon me, 65 ter number 1D898, page 18 in e-court, which should be transcript page 2405 [Realtime transcript read in error "2450"] of the Popovic proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And starting at line 1, sir, I will ask you to follow along with me for the calculations that you performed at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, it's 2405, isn't it, that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "The question I asked you to follow on from that is, when you say that you saw more than 300, 350 men singled out, that is the number that you saw actually taken, not the number you saw taken away before your intervention? "A. No. That is the total estimation of the number of men being singled out during the day. "Q. Well, I'm interested about that because Madam Fauveau did establish with you yesterday that the number you saw in the house on the first day was between, I think you said, 15 and 50. Yes? "A. Yes. I remember that, yes. "Q. And the number you saw in the White House on the second day was between 50 and 100, wasn't it? "A. Yes. I remember that, yes. "Q. So in effect, the number of men you saw placed in those two houses over the course of two days was a maximum of 150. "A. The men I saw at that stage resemble more or less the figure of 150, but when I look at the two days, the whole days, thinking and making an estimation of the men that were singled out, it resembles a higher number. But I was not there at the White House the second day the whole time and I don't know if there were earlier transports before my arrival there." First of all, sir, do you confirm and stand by this selection of your prior testimony as being truthful and accurate as to its contents?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's truthful and accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, others that you saw being singled out may have been later released by the Serbs without you knowing it. Is that another reason that the number in the White House could be less than the total number you saw being selected?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that is the reason. The reason I already explained during the prior testimony is that I was not the whole time at the site of the White House.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And is it accurate that on the 13th of July, the morning when you started the bus evacuations before the Serbs showed up, that approximately 100 to 150 Bosnian Muslim males made it out on those convoys before the Serbs arrived?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the estimations of the numbers. I know that the NIOD report has made some estimations about the number of Muslim men that have made it through and I know they also have found a few men and had some testimonies from them to show what the situation was at the time, but that could be right. I hope there were more, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm relying upon the figure of 100 to 150 Muslim men that you gave in the Popovic trial at transcript page 2318. Was that based on the NIOD report or on your own knowledge? And if you want, we can have that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's 1D897, and it's the bottom of page 7 and the top of page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at the bottom, the question starts at line 19 and your answer begins at line 25, sir. And when you indicate, we can go on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. You can go on to it the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does that refresh your recollection of the figure that I mentioned, 100 or 150 Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refreshes my recollection of the testimony in the Popovic case, and if I'm correct, the Popovic case was before the NIOD report had been revealed. And I don't know what the estimation of the NIOD report is based on my estimation or they made their own calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So what is your estimation based upon then? Would it be your own --

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My observation and estimation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to move to a few areas I have left. First you describe an incident with with a young boy almost being strangled by a Serb in black uniform --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page reference, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 81, line -- I think it's corrected now. I apologise. It was probably due to my speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about an incident where you say a young boy was almost being strangled by a Serb in a black uniform. Do you recall that as soon as you intervened with Mane to tell him what was happening, that he stopped the Serb in the black uniform, told you that you were right for objecting to this, and told the Serb that is he a Serb soldier and should not be there and took him away from that location?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And apart from this one incident, am I correct that you personally did not see any mistreatment or wrongful acts on the part of the Serbs during the evacuation of refugees or the separation of men?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to mistreatment or wrongful acts, of course, there were multiple days filled with mistreatments and wrongful acts. When it comes to specific incidents and the separation of men, of course, I was in the middle of that and had to view and be -- be a part of -- of those -- those incidents. So the almost strangling of the young boy is something that is an incident where I was literally involved and there were multiple incidents where I, of course, tried to convince Mane to let men stay with their families. So if you conclude that there was only one incident in those -- in that period of time, I must say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call 1D900; page 16 in English and page 14 of the B/C/S. And this is again the briefing statement given to the Royal Dutch Army in 1995. And it's again page 16 in English, page 14 of the B/C/S. And it's the second-to-last paragraph that begins "he believed" and says: "He believed that it would have been impossible for the Serbs to have done anything to the refugees which would not have been noticed. This would have been noticed because panic at least would have broken out among the Muslims. They would have also shouted and screamed. The Muslims immediately panicked whenever they saw something, like when the Muslim hanged himself." Do you confirm that this selection is truthful and accurate as to the facts contained therein?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are accurate, and they refer to, if I'm not mistaken, a question about the -- the evening and the night of the 12th, going on to the 13th. And the question was that during the night or the evening, if the Serbs would have come back and did something to Muslim refugees without us noticing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look two -- three paragraphs -- three paragraphs prior on this same page in English, you were talking about the men at the White House and the quote there says: "He did not see any men mistreated there [sic]." Is that a truthful and accurate account of the facts as you know them?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's truthful and accurate if you see it in the light that while I was there, no one was beaten or strangled or whatever. The -- could have happened. So while I was there and present, at the time there was no physical contact between Serbs or Muslim men that were at the White House.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could turn to the next page of this document, there is an item that says: "Treatment of civilians/refugees." And I believe it's the second item from the top. And it is quoted there that you said: "As far as he could tell, reasonably good." Do you confirm that this section from your debriefing accurately and truthfully describes the Serb treatment of the refugees at Potocari as being reasonably good as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to read part of this as the whole document. In the whole document, I don't know how many pages the debriefing in -- in Assen, my personal debriefing took, but in all those pages, all the incidents we have been talking yesterday and today are described. So this is a statement which you have to read in the context of the whole document. So next to the mistreatments and other things I have witnessed, there is nothing else to -- to -- to note.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, sir, and that's where my confusion lays [sic]. The only mistreatment that I have seen identified in your debriefings in your prior testimony was in relation to the one person that almost strangled a Bosnian Muslim that we just went through and everywhere else it says that you did not personally eye-witness any other mistreatment. And that's why I asked you if you had personally eye-witnessed any other mistreatment apart from that incident. I'm asking you again now, sir, if you recall that the incident with the boy was the only mistreatment that you eye-witnessed?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at it in a way that shelling of people, shooting at them, driving them from their homes, breaking up families and forcing them to move from one location to another is not a mistreatment, then I think you're mistaken, because I also see that as mistreatment. But next to that, next to the whole scale of the atrocities, there is this -- the mistreatment I viewed myself. That's the mistreatment of the boy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, people shooting, shelling, forces moving from one location to another, are those not also factors of a war?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are factors of a war. Doesn't mean they are not -- that they are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that the only bodies you saw were -- were described as yourself as being as a result of the hostilities and having nothing to do with the transportation of refugees?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The bodies that I saw were also in other locations than where the transportation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to the incident of the encounters with General Mladic. First of all, the first incident you described where General Mladic talked about the Netherlands and about the prediction that in ten years he would be assisting the Dutch to protect themselves. You indicated that this was translated for you by a Serb translator. Was this translator Miki, who we have identified previously?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not Miki. I believe it was the translator that was always with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would that have been Colonel Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to move to the other incident where your UN translator that you have described had an encounter with General Mladic. And, first of all, am I correct that the entirety of General Mladic's words were conveyed and interpreted to you by that UN translator?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just wondering how much more time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't think I can get it done in under 25 minutes. So I think I'll need about 25 minutes to view the three short clips and complete the short questions that I have on the encounter with General Mladic and on the -- Miki, the translator, and the discussions with Mane, and those are the only two topics that I have remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Van Duijn, unfortunately, it will not be able to finish today, to conclude today, although we would have wished to do so, as you may have understood. Nevertheless, in view of the time assessment given in advance by the Defence, the Chamber considers it fair that they have an opportunity to conclude your testimony tomorrow. I'm sorry for you that you have to return, although for a short period of time, tomorrow morning. Meanwhile, I would like to instruct you again that you should not speak or communicate with anyone about your testimony, and most likely we'll be done in the first session tomorrow morning, so you can make your plans on from -- after -- after the morning session. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: See you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for the day, when there's no matter to be raised at this moment, and we'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 26th of April, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 26th day of April, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.17 p.m.,
